text: Minerals serve three major roles: structural material for bones, nerve impulse transmission, and driving body chemical reactions (digestion, muscle contraction, immune function). Calcium (about 2% of body weight, 99% stored in the skeleton) is essential for bone, eggshell, and growth; dried shell powder is a good source, but vitamin D is needed for proper absorption; deficiency causes rickets in poultry, cattle, and swine, and in layers specifically causes thin eggshells and lower egg production (oyster shell powder helps). Cattle and sows need a lot of calcium during milk production — right after delivery, calcium demand can be high enough to cause weakness and paralysis, requiring a calcium gluconate injection from a vet. Phosphorus (80% stored in bone) works alongside calcium for bone and muscle development and is important for reproduction; it's usually supplied together with calcium — DCP (Di-Calcium Phosphate) is a good combined source; avoid natural phosphates from rice fields, which contain toxic fluorine. Magnesium acts similarly to phosphorus and alongside calcium in many body chemical reactions; deficiency causes tremor, muscle weakness, and nervousness (sources: cereals, molasses). Iron: piglets have limited iron reserves at birth and sow's milk cannot supply enough, so piglets face iron deficiency after about 7 days without supplementation — inject Iron Dextran (well absorbed) on day 2 of life with a booster 10 days later to prevent anemia.
